screens.title: Testing Smart Contracts with Truffle Tests
screens.subtitle: Why tests are mandatory, and how to write and run JavaScript tests with Mocha and Chai in Truffle

narration.text: Smart contracts run immutable code on a shared network and often control real funds. That means testing is not optional — it's a safety system. In this lesson you will learn the structure of Truffle tests, why JavaScript tests with Mocha and Chai are the practical choice, and the habits that make tests reliable. We'll step through a SimpleStorage example, show how to deploy fresh instances for isolation, how to assert values safely when blockchain types appear, and how to run and interpret the truffle test output. You will also see common mistakes that cause flaky tests, like forgetting to await asynchronous calls or reusing the same contract instance across tests. By the end you will understand not only how to write tests, but why certain test patterns, such as using beforeEach with Contract. new(), are essential for preventing order-dependent failures. Think of tests as the contract's unit armor: they catch logic regressions early and build confidence before deployment. As you watch the examples, consider how each test isolates state and why that matters for reproducible results.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Testing smart contracts with Truffle, Mocha, and Chai prevents irreversible errors by verifying behavior in isolated, repeatable test runs.

screens.title: Why testing is mandatory for smart contracts
screens.subtitle: Testing protects immutable code that can control real value

narration.text: Smart contracts operate on blockchains where deployed code cannot be changed. That immutability elevates testing from a best practice to a safety requirement. A bug in production is not simply an inconvenience — it can allow funds to be stolen or lock assets permanently. Testing verifies intended behavior across scenarios: initial states, successful flows, unsuccessful flows, and boundary cases. In practice, this means writing tests that cover normal updates, edge conditions, and negative cases that should revert. For example, a SimpleStorage contract that sets and gets a numeric value should be tested not only for correct set and get behavior but also for multiple sequential updates and starting default values. A common misconception is that small contracts do not need tests; in fact, small contracts still enforce rules or hold value and can still break. Another misconception is that passing a few manual checks suffices; automated tests run quickly, can be repeated before every commit, and serve as living documentation of expected behavior. When you write tests, think of them as executable specifications that both protect users and speed debugging. Ask yourself: if a function were called in an unexpected order, do my tests show what should happen? That question helps guide test coverage and prevents costly surprises after deployment.

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: Testing prevents irreversible errors by ensuring code behaves correctly in many scenarios, including edge cases and repeated state changes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Why testing is mandatory
Definition

Testing smart contracts means writing automated checks that verify contract behavior under many scenarios, including normal operation, edge cases, and failure modes that should revert.

Analogy
Think of tests as safety harnesses: they let you refactor and deploy with confidence because they catch regressions early.
Common misconception
Small contracts don't need tests — false. Even trivial logic can be exploited, so tests are always valuable.
Key Takeaway

Treat tests as the primary defense for immutable contracts. Automate them early and run them frequently to catch regressions before deployment.

Concrete example: SimpleStorage
// test/SimpleStorage.test.js
const SimpleStorage = artifacts.require("SimpleStorage");

contract("SimpleStorage", (accounts) => {
  let simpleStorageInstance;
  beforeEach(async () => { simpleStorageInstance = await SimpleStorage.new(); });

  it("should retrieve initial value as 0", async () => {
    const initial = await simpleStorageInstance.get();
    assert.equal(initial.toNumber(), 0);
  });
});
This short test verifies the default state and uses a fresh instance per test to guarantee independence.
Try this
Write a test that sets a value, updates it twice, and asserts both intermediate and final values to confirm state changes work as expected.

screens.title: Truffle's testing stack: Mocha and Chai
screens.subtitle: How the pieces fit together inside Truffle tests

narration.text: Truffle integrates two widely used JavaScript testing libraries to give you structure and assertions. Mocha provides the test runner and the structure for suites and cases: contract blocks act like describes and it blocks describe behaviors. Chai supplies assertion helpers such as assert. equal or expect-style assertions to compare values. Truffle wraps this integration and injects a test environment that deploys contracts to an in-memory blockchain or a configured Ganache instance and provides a list of accounts for transaction simulation. When you call artifacts. require in a test file, Truffle loads the contract abstraction so you can deploy with Contract. new() or interact with an instance. A typical flow is: load contract abstraction, use a beforeEach hook to deploy a fresh instance, then inside each it block call contract functions and assert outcomes. A common misconception is that Truffle hides asynchronous behavior; it does not — you must await asynchronous calls for transactions and view functions. Another misconception is that Truffle automatically isolates state across it blocks; only fresh deployments ensure that isolation. Understanding this stack helps you write tests that are readable, maintainable, and practically useful for debugging and documenting contract expectations.

keyIdea.title: Testing stack
keyIdea.text: Mocha structures tests, Chai makes assertions, and Truffle supplies the blockchain simulation and contract abstractions to run them.

screens.title: Writing JavaScript tests: structure and example
screens.subtitle: A complete SimpleStorage.test.js walkthrough

narration.text: Let's walk through a representative JavaScript test file for a SimpleStorage contract. Start by loading the contract abstraction using artifacts. require. That gives you a handle to deploy or interact with instances. Then define a contract block which is a Truffle wrapper around Mocha's describe that injects accounts. Inside the contract block declare a variable to hold the contract instance and use a beforeEach hook to deploy a fresh instance with Contract. new(). This ensures test isolation. Each it block then describes expected behavior and performs actions: call set with a value from an account, await the transaction, then await the getter and assert its value. Remember to convert returned BigNumber values with toNumber before comparing. A concrete test might set 100, read it back, and assert equality. Also add a test that confirms the initial value is zero. Finally, add a multi-update test that sets 50 then 75, asserting after each call that the contract returns the expected intermediate and final values. The structure is straightforward but disciplined: load, deploy fresh state, act, and assert. This pattern keeps your tests readable and robust. One misconception to avoid is testing by mutating shared state between tests; always prefer fresh deployments for predictable results.

keyIdea.title: Test pattern
keyIdea.text: Load contract, deploy new instance in beforeEach, then in each it block act and assert, converting types as needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Code Walkthrough
Test file anatomy
  • Load contract abstraction with artifacts.require("SimpleStorage").
  • Use contract("SimpleStorage", (accounts) => { ... }) to get the injected accounts array.
  • Deploy a fresh instance in beforeEach with SimpleStorage.new() to ensure isolation.
  • In it blocks, call functions with await and assert results after converting BigNumber values.
Common mistake
Using SimpleStorage.deployed() in beforeEach shares the same instance across tests and leads to order-dependent failures.
// test/SimpleStorage.test.js const SimpleStorage = artifacts.require("SimpleStorage"); contract("SimpleStorage", (accounts) => { let simpleStorageInstance; beforeEach(async () => { simpleStorageInstance = await SimpleStorage.new(); }); it("should set the value of storedData correctly", async () => { const expectedValue = 100; await simpleStorageInstance.set(expectedValue, { from: accounts[0] }); const actualValue = await simpleStorageInstance.get(); assert.equal(actualValue.toNumber(), expectedValue, "The value was not stored correctly."); }); });
Quick example
Test that sets 100, reads back the value, and asserts equality after converting the returned value to a number.

screens.title: beforeEach and Contract.new(): why isolation matters
screens.subtitle: Deploy fresh contract instances per test to avoid flaky suites

narration.text: Test isolation ensures that each test starts from a predictable state. Truffle tests commonly use a beforeEach hook that deploys a new contract instance with Contract. new() before each it block. This pattern prevents side effects from earlier tests, such as modified storage values or changed balances, from contaminating later ones. A typical anti-pattern is using Contract. deployed() inside beforeEach; that returns the same migrated instance, making tests order-dependent. Order dependence creates flakiness: tests pass when run alone but fail when run together or in a different sequence. Isolation also makes failures easier to diagnose because each failing test can be run independently with the same starting state. A concrete way to see the difference is to write two tests that change the stored value and observe that using the same instance causes the second test to inherit state from the first, while deploying new instances keeps tests independent. Remember to await Contract. new() and any transactions inside it so the deployment completes before the it block executes. Isolation is a simple habit with a big payoff: predictable, repeatable test results and faster debugging.

keyIdea.title: Isolation principle
keyIdea.text: Deploying a fresh contract instance in beforeEach avoids order-dependent failures and makes tests deterministic and debuggable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Test Isolation
What beforeEach does
beforeEach runs before every it test case. When you call Contract.new() inside it, Truffle deploys a new contract instance for each test so state does not carry between tests.
Anti-pattern
Using Contract.deployed() in beforeEach shares an instance across tests and causes state leakage.
Benefit
Fresh instances mean tests are independent, easier to reproduce, and quicker to debug when they fail.
Check your understanding
If two tests modify the same contract state, what will happen when you use Contract.deployed() in beforeEach? The second test may observe the first test's changes, causing flaky, order-dependent failures.
Mini example
beforeEach(async () => {
  // good
  simpleStorageInstance = await SimpleStorage.new();
});

// vs
beforeEach(async () => {
  // bad: shares instance
  simpleStorageInstance = await SimpleStorage.deployed();
});
Deploying new instances ensures each it block begins from a blank, known state.
Pro tip

If a test fails intermittently, check for shared state and missing await calls first — those are common root causes.

screens.title: Assertions and BigNumber handling
screens.subtitle: Convert blockchain numeric types before comparing values

narration.text: Blockchain numeric types returned from contract calls are often BigNumber objects. These objects are not strictly equal to primitive JavaScript numbers, so a direct assertion comparing a BigNumber to a number can fail even when their numeric values match. The common pattern is to convert the BigNumber to a primitive before comparison, for example by calling toNumber() or toString(), depending on the size and limits of your test values. In our SimpleStorage example, get() returns a BigNumber. After awaiting the getter, call toNumber on the returned value before passing it to assert. equal. This avoids type mismatches and makes the assertion check the numeric content instead of object identity. A practical misconception is assuming JavaScript's == will solve the problem; comparing an object to a primitive is still unreliable and should be avoided. For extremely large integers near JavaScript's numeric limits prefer toString and compare strings to avoid precision issues. As a rule of thumb, convert blockchain numeric values to a comparable primitive type before any equality check in tests, and choose the conversion method that preserves correctness for the values you expect to see.

keyIdea.title: Assertion rule
keyIdea.text: Always convert BigNumber return values to a comparable primitive before asserting equality to avoid false assertion failures.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Assertions & BigNumber
Why conversion matters

BigNumber objects are not equal to primitive numbers. Convert with toNumber() or toString() before comparing to avoid type-based assertion failures.

Recommended
Use actualValue.toNumber() for typical small integers in tests and assert.equal against a JavaScript number.
When to use toString()
For very large integers near numeric limits, compare strings to avoid precision loss in JavaScript numbers.
Misconception
Relying on weak equality conversions can hide type issues. Convert explicitly to a primitive and assert deterministically.
Concrete example
const actualValue = await simpleStorageInstance.get();
// Convert before asserting
assert.equal(actualValue.toNumber(), 100, "The value was not stored correctly.");
This explicit conversion prevents object-vs-primitive mismatches and makes your assertion reflect numeric equality.
Key Takeaway

Always convert blockchain numeric types to a comparable primitive before asserting equality in tests.

screens.title: Running tests with truffle test and reading output
screens.subtitle: From terminal command to pass/fail summary

narration.text: Running your test suite is a single command: truffle test. Truffle first compiles changed contracts, then runs every test file in the project's test directory against a local EVM, such as an in-memory provider or Ganache. The terminal output shows compilation notes, each test suite, and individual test cases with timings and status. Passing tests are reported with a green checkmark or a passing indicator and failing tests show a message describing the assertion that failed. At the end you will see a brief summary indicating the total number of passing tests and the elapsed time. Use that summary to confirm the suite's health after making changes. If a test fails, read its failure message and the stack trace to locate the assertion and map it to the source. A common confusion is interpreting a transaction revert as a failing test; a revert is expected when testing negative cases and should be asserted explicitly by the test. When tests involve asynchronous setup or missing await statements, failures may be timing-related; ensure each await completes before asserting. Running truffle test frequently during development keeps regressions small and makes each failure easier to diagnose.

keyIdea.title: Run & read
keyIdea.text: Use truffle test to compile and run tests, then inspect per-test output and the final summary to diagnose failures quickly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › truffle test
Terminal demo (static)
$ truffle test Compiling your contracts... =========================== > Everything is up to date Contract: SimpleStorage ✓ should set the value of storedData correctly (100ms) ✓ should retrieve the initial value of storedData as 0 (70ms) ✓ should allow multiple updates to storedData (120ms) 3 passing (1s)
This output shows compilation, per-test timing, and a final summary of passing tests. Use the timings to identify slow tests to optimize later.
Diagnosing failures
Look at the failing test message and stack trace, map the assertion to your test file, reproduce the failing case in isolation, then fix the contract or the test accordingly.
Negative-case advice
If a test expects a revert, assert that the revert occurs rather than treating any revert as a failure. Explicit expectations clarify intent and prevent false negatives.
Quick takeaway

Run tests often and read failures carefully; the terminal output is your fastest route to resolving issues before deployment.

screens.title: Common testing pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Practical traps: no await, shared instances, incomplete coverage, and gas issues

narration.text: Several recurring mistakes make smart contract test suites fragile. First, forgetting await on asynchronous calls causes assertions to run before transactions or calls complete, producing misleading failures. Always await deployments, transactions, and view calls. Second, using migrated or shared deployed instances rather than Contract. new in beforeEach leads to shared state and order-dependent tests. Third, relying only on happy-path tests misses edge cases and security issues. Include tests for error conditions and boundary values, such as zero values, negative-like behavior, or reverts. Fourth, incorrect assertions due to BigNumber objects can give false negatives; convert types explicitly before comparing. Finally, gas-limit issues can arise when tests perform expensive operations; although Truffle's test environment has generous defaults, be mindful for complex scenarios and consider increasing gas limits or testing heavy operations in isolated integration tests. To avoid all these traps, follow a checklist: await every async call, deploy a fresh instance per test, convert BigNumbers, write negative-case tests, and monitor test execution times. These practices reduce flakiness and make the suite a trustworthy tool for catching regressions. Common testing pitfalls and how to avoid them means avoid missing awaits, shared instances, poor assertions, shallow coverage, and gas surprises to keep tests reliable.. In practical terms, practical traps: no await, shared instances, incomplete coverage, and gas issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls list
keyIdea.text: Avoid missing awaits, shared instances, poor assertions, shallow coverage, and gas surprises to keep tests reliable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Common Pitfalls
Checklist to avoid flaky tests
  • Await every asynchronous deployment, transaction, or call.
  • Use Contract.new() in beforeEach to deploy fresh instances for each test.
  • Convert BigNumber values to primitives before assertions.
  • Write negative and edge-case tests as well as happy paths.
  • Be mindful of gas for heavy operations and adjust test strategy if needed.
Reflex
When a test fails intermittently, first check for missing await and shared instance usage; those are the most likely causes.
Example failure
Two tests that set a value will conflict if they share the same instance; the second test might read the first test's update and fail its assertions.
Pro tip

Add small, focused tests that assert a single behavior each. They are faster, clearer, and easier to debug than large tests that cover many interactions.

screens.title: Activity: Create and run SimpleStorage tests
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab to write the tests and run truffle test

narration.text: Follow this hands-on sequence to build and run tests for the SimpleStorage contract. First, create a file named SimpleStorage. test. js inside the project's test directory. Load the contract abstraction with artifacts. require and define a contract block that receives accounts. Inside it declare a variable for the contract instance and use beforeEach to deploy a fresh instance with SimpleStorage. new(). Then add three it tests: one that asserts the initial getter returns zero, one that sets a value like 100 and asserts it reads back, and one that performs multiple updates and asserts after each update. Remember to await both the set transaction and the get call, and call toNumber() on returned values before comparing. Run truffle test in your terminal with Ganache running or using Truffle's in-memory provider. Observe the passing tests and the final summary. If a test fails, reproduce it in isolation, check for missing await or incorrect instance usage, and inspect assertion conversions. This exercise reinforces patterns: isolation, awaiting async operations, correct assertion types, and interpreting the test output to fix bugs. Try introducing a deliberate bug in the contract to see the test fail, then fix the contract and confirm the test passes.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Core takeaways from testing with Truffle

narration.text: Keep four core ideas in mind when testing smart contracts with Truffle. First, testing is essential because deployed contracts are immutable and can hold value. Second, Truffle uses Mocha for structure and Chai for assertions, while providing artifacts and an EVM for local runs. Third, deploy fresh instances with Contract. new() inside beforeEach to ensure test isolation. Fourth, convert BigNumber return values to primitives before asserting equality to avoid false failures. These practices form the backbone of a reliable testing workflow. As you continue, treat tests as executable documentation: they describe expected behavior, run quickly, and make regressions obvious. Use this checklist when writing tests: await every async call, deploy fresh instances per test, compare converted values, and include both happy and negative paths. These steps will drastically reduce surprises when you deploy real contracts to public networks.

keyIdea.title: Core checklist
keyIdea.text: Await calls, isolate tests with Contract.new(), convert BigNumbers, and cover edge cases for dependable test suites.

Summary takeaway

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three one-line reminders to use when writing tests

narration.text: Keep these three concise reminders handy while you write tests. First: always await asynchronous calls and transactions to ensure state changes complete before assertions. Second: deploy a fresh contract instance in beforeEach using Contract. new() to maintain test isolation. Third: convert BigNumber return values to primitives before comparing them in assertions. These three small habits prevent the majority of flaky test problems and make your suite faster to diagnose and more reliable as part of your development workflow. When you get into the habit of following them, test failures will point to real logic issues rather than setup mistakes. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means await async calls, isolate tests with new deployments, and convert bignumbers before asserting.. In practical terms, three one-line reminders to use when writing tests. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: Await async calls, isolate tests with new deployments, and convert BigNumbers before asserting.

content.html:

Ensure deployments, transactions, and calls are awaited before assertions run.

Final thought

These three quick rules make your test suite robust and your contract deployments safer.
